cross_item_rule: The only rule that repeatedly fired was a coherence check internal to an option, not a shape tell: where an option pairs a named thing with a claimed property (19: temper type vs. what firing does to it; 13: humidity setting vs. cure behaviour; 17: a named process vs. its standard form), real-world knowledge kills the incoherent pairings. It fired on 3 of 24 items and never got below two legal options, because in every case the item's 2x2 scramble leaves both coherent pairings standing. It did NOT fire on the pure-number notes items (1, 3, 5, 6, 10, 14, 18, 21): those hold every option in one identical frame varying only a figure or a subset, so every option satisfies the stem equally and only the withheld notes discriminate. On the 13 transition items there is no signal of any kind - the options are bare connectives and the text is the whole question. Standard structural proxies (lone absolute, lone long option, odd party named, broken frame) fired on zero items: the frames are uniform by construction.
shared_frames: Three families. (a) Transitions: 2, 4, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 15, 16, 20, 22, 23, 24 - identical stem, four bare connectives; solving one tells you nothing about another. (b) Number-substitution notes items: 1, 3, 5, 21 (and 18 as a paired variant) - one sentence held fixed with a single figure swapped; same construction, no transfer. (c) 2x2 scrambles where two attributes are crossed: 6, 13, 18, 19, 21. Recognising that construction helps in general (it tells you the wrong options include internally impossible pairings) and is what makes 19 and 13 partly attackable, but it does not transfer an answer from one item to another. (d) Trajectory-shape items: 10 and 17 share a frame - fixed endpoints, four different paths between them - and 17 is attackable by domain knowledge while 10 is not.
